231:## Contradictions
232-<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). Full discussion: reports/methodology-comparison.md §4. -->
233:- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. Pass 2: on 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions a fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul beats all 8 zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; with an argmax decision rule the same detector looks like always-safe (0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845 [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. [I] A conservative threshold is consistent with Ding's fine-tuned models labelling both pair members benign in 84–88% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; unpaired and pair-wise results must not be pooled.
234:- **C2 RepoAudit.** Own paper: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision), all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Independent study: 0/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7], 92.77% SFDR on real-world projects [@li2026llm, p. 11], average $172.77 per project, max $1,247.66 [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Differs in targets (prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs), version (old commits vs current HEAD; the 5 overlapping modules only in li's real-world set), metric (precision vs recall/SFDR), labeller (authors vs Codex), bug types and scale. [I] Dependence on source/sink API coverage (zero-token runs; API modelling explains 108/108 misses [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]). Unresolved.
235:- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner. Pass 2: on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions LLMs lead on balanced accuracy, but at 1:44 prevalence Flawfinder (6.2–13.4%) and Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9) are more precise than every LLM (2.3–4.6%), while Cppcheck sits in the LLM range [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The families fail in opposite directions (LLMs over-flag, SAST finds little), so the ranking depends on the metric.
236:- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only. Pass 2, against: reasoning lowers DeepSeek-V3.2 specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20], while it helps frontier models' balanced accuracy. [I] Model-dependent.
237:- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment. Pass 2: deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; in tashenova changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
238:- **C6 IRIS hybrid.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8], but on real-world Java IRIS SFDR is 97.80% vs CodeQL 77.00% [@li2026llm, p. 12]. Not like-for-like (known CVEs vs new code; detections vs SFDR; labelling). [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. Open.
239:- **C7 Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score.** LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul: F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12] vs CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Neither paper explains the 28-point gap. [I] Likely split and preprocessing differences (lu used LineVul's original pipeline [@lu2025lab, p. 8]); in-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers.
240:- **C8 Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive?** CodeBERT-PrimeVul on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 (F1 ≈ 0.15 at 1:44, our calculation) [@deininger2026open, p. 11], while BigVul/ICVul/Devign/Juliet-trained DL on post-May-2025 VentiVul falls to F1 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. [I] Differences in dataset (VentiVul 2025 CVEs, Whole-File units), training data quality (PrimeVul vs BigVul) and threshold policy; unresolved.
241-
242:## Agreements / converging evidence
243-- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. Pass 2: on post-May-2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]; at 1:44, LLM precision 2.3–4.6% vs flag-all 2.21% [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; on real WordPress PHP CVEs best macro-F1 0.601 [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
244-- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.) Pass 2: only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels are genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
245-- **G3 Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).** GPT-4 two-shot labels both pair members vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8]; dual-agent flags 88.2% [@tan2026think, p. 7]; always-vulnerable rows among khare's best F1 [@khare2025understanding, p. 16]. Partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
246-- **G4 SAST recall is low on real code, high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** Best single tools 30.0–44.4%, many 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]; CodeQL recall 6.00–34.29% C/C++ and 14.19% Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]; CodeQL 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8]; CASTLE CodeQL 29%, SAST average 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]; vs CodeQL accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
252:- **G10 Trivial baselines are competitive (moderate).** A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings and is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]; always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615 [@deininger2026open, p. 7]; all-positive F1 3.87% vs most LLM F1 on VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 14]; shu2026evaluating also reports all-vulnerable and all-clean dummy baselines [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11]. [I] Few papers report such baselines; most headline numbers are never compared to one.
253:- **G11 Cost per true positive (moderate, single study).** USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude Sonnet 5) and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44, excluding human triage of 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; Qwen/Llama kJ/TP use FLOP estimates, not measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

## Positioning of our review

**Question.** Does a review or SLR already compare LLM-based, SAST and DL vulnerability detection through an evaluation-setup / benchmark-realism lens, i.e. arguing that benchmark design explains contradictory results?

**Verdict.** We found no review that does both of the following (searches on 2026-11-12: Q1–Q5, Q21, Q22, W1, W2):
1. synthesises head-to-head evidence across all three families (LLM, SAST, DL) **plus** LLM+SAST hybrids;
2. explains specific contradictions between primary studies through their evaluation setup, with a cross-paper comparability audit.

Several reviews cover parts of this, so the claim of novelty must be narrow and precise. **Confidence: medium.** The closest competing review (qin2026review, the CAI 2026 review) has now been read in full and confirms the difference (see below). The other near-miss reviews were read at abstract level only, and the field publishes very fast.

**The four reviews in our corpus.**

| Review | What it covers | How our review differs |
|---|---|---|
| kaniewski2026systematic (TOSEM SLR, 263 studies to Nov 2025) | LLM-based detection only. Deep analysis of datasets, custom splits and leakage [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35; @kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38]. Excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8]. | It does not cover the LLM-filters-SAST family (C2) and does not synthesise LLM-vs-SAST results. [I] None of its future directions calls for same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38]. Its research directions recommend SAST+LLM pipelines [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 42], so our evidence on them complements it. |
| zhou2025large (TOSEM SLR, 58 studies to Mar 2024) | LLMs for detection and repair, taxonomy of adaptation techniques. | It predates almost all hybrid, agentic and project-scale evidence. Only one of 40 detection studies was repository-level [@zhou2025large, p. 18]. Its only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own preprint [@zhou2025large, p. 22]. |
| sheng2025llms (ACM CSUR narrative survey, 58 studies 2019–2024) | Techniques, datasets and challenges, including leakage and label errors [@sheng2025llms, p. 25]. | It is narrative. It neither compares families on matched results nor ties contradictions to setup. [I] |
| qin2026review (Computers and Artificial Intelligence 2026, Zeus Press; single-author narrative review, 32 references). **The closest competing review.** | Same evaluation-reliability framing as ours: benchmark gains inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits and temporal leakage [@qin2026review, p. 1; @qin2026review, p. 10] [A]. Recommends out-of-time and project-isolated testing, recall at a fixed false-positive budget, audit time per real vulnerability, and SAST-LLM systems evaluated by total audit cost [@qin2026review, p. 13] [A]. | [I] No search protocol, screening or quality assessment (pp. 1–4 report none). SAST is explicitly out of scope [@qin2026review, p. 4], yet it draws an LLM-vs-SAST conclusion [@qin2026review, p. 12] whose only head-to-head source found LLMs above SAST on F1 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. Its quantitative claims rest on ding2025vulnerability, gnieciak2025large and sheng2025llms [@qin2026review, p. 15], all in our corpus, so it is **not independent evidence**. It does not map contradictions study by study onto evaluation setup. Venue peer review is not documented. |

None of the four pools or re-scores performance numbers (methodology comparison §2-F) [I]. qin2026review strengthens our novelty claim rather than weakening it: it shares the framing but provides neither the cross-family scope nor the contradiction audit [I].

**Closest reviews outside our corpus** (not analysed, abstract only, found via Q1–Q5, Q21, Q22, Q26, W1, W2):
- *[SoK] Large Language Models in Security Code Review and Testing*, Journal of Systems Research 2026, doi:10.5070/sr3.62177. Covers LLMs in detection, fuzzing and exploit generation "including a comparison with tools that follow traditional approaches". It is broader than our scope, and its abstract shows no benchmark-realism lens.
- *Modern Approaches to Software Vulnerability Detection: A Survey of ML, DL, and LLMs*, Electronics 2025, doi:10.3390/electronics14224449. Covers ML → DL → LLM, metrics and challenges such as class imbalance and the lack of real datasets. SAST appears only as motivation. Its abstract shows no head-to-head or contradiction analysis.
- *The Data Problem in Software Vulnerability Analysis: Artifacts, Quality, and Consumption*, 2026 preprint, doi:10.13140/rg.2.2.23928.40963. A dataset-centric review of realism, label evidence and leakage over 1,522 papers. It is the closest to our "benchmark realism" lens, but it reviews datasets, not comparative detector performance.
- Other near misses:
  - *LLMs for Software Vulnerability Detection: A Survey of Methods, Evaluation, and Future Trends* (GAIIS 2026, doi:10.1109/gaiis69281.2026.11519183): 32 LLM-only studies.
  - *A Systematic Literature Review of Traditional and LLM Approaches to Static Code Analysis for Bug Detection* (TechRxiv preprint 2025, doi:10.36227/techrxiv.175976382.24840067/v1): 11 papers, general bugs.
  - *LLMs and Agentic AI for Vulnerability Management: A Systematic Review* (Expert Systems 2026, doi:10.1111/exsy.70437): covers the whole management lifecycle.
  - *Large Language Models for Cyber Security: A Systematic Literature Review* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3769676): broad security scope.
  - *A systematic literature Review for Transformer-based Software Vulnerability detection* (arXiv 2604.24822): Transformers only.
  - *Pitfalls in Language Models for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): a generic pitfalls taxonomy.

**How our review should position itself** [I]:
1. **Cross-family scope.** It covers all three families plus both hybrid types (C1, C2), which none of the reviews above combines.
2. **Contradiction-driven synthesis.** Six named contradictions are each traced to differences in metric, data, unit, labeller or scoring (methodology comparison §4). Examples:
   - fine-tuned models vs GPT-4 reverse between Big-Vul F1 and PrimeVul pairwise scoring [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9];
   - class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40];
   - scoring leniency favours LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6].
3. **Explicit comparability audit.** We state which cross-paper numbers may and may not be compared (§3). For example, CodeQL on OWASP replicates across two groups [@khare2025understanding, p. 9; @xiong2026sifting, p. 11], while Big-Vul F1 is not comparable.
4. **Page-level verification and baseline checks.** We check results against trivial baselines (W1), which reviews of headline numbers do not do.

**Risk.** With 24 papers (20 primary studies), the review must be framed as a *critical comparative review*, not a comprehensive SLR. Reviewers will likely point to qin2026review (the CAI 2026 review) and kaniewski2026systematic for the "evaluation pitfalls" message. The distinct contribution is the cross-family, contradiction-explaining angle, and the G1 re-analysis below would make it concrete.

## G1: Published results are not re-scored against trivial baselines or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists for comparing LLMs, SAST and DL
- Gap type: methodological
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Results sit at the flag-everything level.** On 50/50 data, "flag everything" gives F1 0.667. Studies with balanced data report best values at or below that level:
    - shu: the dummy classifier scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11; @shu2026evaluating, p. 17] [V];
    - tan: best F1 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7];
    - yildiz: GPT F1 48–66 [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6];
    - khare: always-vulnerable rows appear among the best F1 values [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
  - **The same pattern holds at other prevalences, in three more recent studies** (second pass). Two of them report trivial baselines themselves; for the third the chance level is derivable:
    - deininger (35.4% vulnerable sample): LLM F1 0.405–0.615 against always-vulnerable F1 0.523 [@deininger2026open, p. 7] [V]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% against 2.21% for always-flag, with 25.6–41.9 false positives per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V] (2.8–4.6% in the budget-matched second epoch [@deininger2026open, p. 17]).
    - tashenova (PHP): a one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats the TF-IDF random forest in 4 of 6 settings and is within 0.001 macro-F1 of the Bi-LSTM [@tashenova2026real, p. 8] [V]. The authors ask that future detectors "be required to clear such trivial baselines" [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A].
    - lu (VentiVul, post-May-2025 CVEs, prevalence 263/13,326 = 1.97% [@lu2025lab, p. 4]): DL F1 is 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13] [V]. The paper reports no trivial baseline; by our calculation the all-positive F1 is 3.87%, and 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below it [@lu2025lab, p. 14] [I].
  - **Class balance flips rankings.**
    - shu: fine-tuned GPT-4o wins on balanced data, but PLMs win on the 17%-vulnerable test [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
    - yildiz: F1 falls from about 49–65 to 5.41–12.21 on non-paired data [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7] [V].
  - **Scoring is unequal between families.**
    - gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6] [V].
    - The CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring scheme to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9] [V].
    - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8] [V].
  - **Headline LLM-vs-SAST numbers use five incompatible metrics**: macro F1, CASTLE score, accuracy, detection ratio, recall/SFDR [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @zhou2024comparison, p. 5; @li2026llm, p. 11] [I].
  - **Spurious baselines and random references:**
    - a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11] [V];
    - GPT-4 pairwise correctness is below the 22.70% random reference [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9] [V].
  - **Statistics are rare.** Among the first 16 primary studies, only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count]. Of the four second-pass papers, deininger2026open uses a paired bootstrap with Holm correction [@deininger2026open, p. 6] [V].
  - **The decision rule and the prompt can flip conclusions.** At the default argmax threshold the fine-tuned PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe despite ROC-AUC 0.845; the authors nearly reported this as "trained detectors are no better than LLMs" [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [V]. Prompt paraphrases change the winning LLM [@deininger2026open, p. 20] [V].
  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A]. lu2025lab asks for cross-dataset and temporally separated testing plus patch-pair metrics [@lu2025lab, p. 16] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q4, Q5, Q9, Q10 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025 and W4; second pass Q35 on OpenAlex/Crossref from 2025). Closest work:
  - **In our corpus, within-study baselines only.** shu2026evaluating, deininger2026open and tashenova2026real report trivial baselines, and lu2025lab's chance level is derivable (see evidence above). PrimeVul's VD-S is also in the corpus. Each applies the baseline only to its own results; none re-scores other studies [I].
  - **qin2026review** (in corpus) recommends better reporting [@qin2026review, p. 13] but recomputes no published results; its only quantitative re-report repeats ding2025vulnerability's table [@qin2026review, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7] [I].
  - *Pitfalls in Machine Learning for Computer Security* (CACM 2024, doi:10.1145/3643456) and *Pitfalls in LMs for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): generic pitfall catalogues with no re-scoring of vulnerability-detection results.
  - *How much model does warning triage need?* (American Impact Review 2026, doi:10.66308/air.e80134906): re-scores models against a simple reference with MCC and bootstrap CIs, but for actionable-warning triage, not vulnerability detection, and in an unknown-tier venue.
  - *On-premise open-weight LLMs for interpretable web vulnerability detection* (TSARKA Science 2026, doi:10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11; abstract only, from Q32): notes that several configurations "approach the score of a classifier labelling every input as vulnerable" and proposes reporting specificity. Again within one study (120 snippets).
  - Q35 returned no relevant hit.

  We found no study that recomputes published LLM, SAST and DL vulnerability-detection results *across studies* against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (searches on 2026-11-12).
- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged (still open).** Trivial baselines are spreading as a *within-study* practice. This makes the gap's premise stronger: four further studies (deininger, tashenova, lu, and the abstract-only TSARKA study) show results at or near trivial levels. It does not fill the gap, because none of them re-scores other studies' published numbers on a common scale [I]. The contribution should now be framed as a *systematic cross-study* re-scoring, and it must credit these within-study baselines rather than claim to be the first to use them.
- Confidence: **medium–high**. The evidence now comes from ≥9 independent primary studies. The only risk is an unpublished or non-indexed meta-analysis.
- Potential contribution: a "re-scored results table" that makes the review's central claim concrete. Many reported LLM advantages may vanish or reverse once compared with flag-all baselines and evaluated at realistic prevalence. It also yields a minimal reporting checklist (confusion matrix, prevalence, trivial baselines, unit and location rule, runs/variance).
- Suggested study (secondary analysis of published numbers; no model runs):
  - **Data:** results tables of the 20 primary studies (plus any added papers). Extract every (study, tool, dataset, configuration) row that reports enough to rebuild a confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN, or P, R and prevalence.
  - **Sample:** all extractable rows. Rows without prevalence or FPR are listed separately, not dropped silently.
  - **Method:** for each row compute:
    - MCC;
    - Youden's J = recall − FPR;
    - ΔF1 = F1 − F1_flag-all, where F1_flag-all = 2π/(1+π) and π is prevalence;
    - precision at deployment prevalence (π = 1%, 5%, 17%) via P = R·π / (R·π + FPR·(1−π)).
  - **Baselines:** always-vulnerable; random (P-C reference 22.70% for ding-style pairs); published dummy, word-count or token-count baselines where available. Use a study's own published baseline where it exists (shu, deininger, tashenova) and check that our formula reproduces it; this is a built-in validity check of the re-scoring.
  - **Analysis:** within each study, rank tools before and after re-scoring and count rank reversals (Kendall τ). Do not pool across datasets marked "not comparable" in methodology comparison §3. Report how many rows fail to beat flag-all.
  - **Threats:** many rows lack TN/FPR (selection bias); rounding in published tables; lenient TP definitions cannot be undone after the fact; transcription errors (mitigate by double extraction and spot-checking against PDFs).
- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy**. Needs only a spreadsheet or about 50 lines of Python, no GPU and no API cost, and takes about 2–4 weeks. It can be included directly in the comparative review as an added-value table.

38:- Confidence: **medium** (narrowed). The remaining gap is more specific, so it is easier to defend, but near misses now lack only one or two conditions (post-cutoff, context, semantic SAST). Re-check before submission.
40:- Suggested study:
41:  - **Data:** Python (build-free for SAST) or Java CVEs. Collect vulnerability-fixing commits from GitHub Security Advisories/OSV (CVEfixes or MoreFixes pipeline). Split into a *post-cutoff* set (disclosed after the newest evaluated model's training cutoff) and a *pre-cutoff* set of the same size.
42:  - **Sample:** about 100 post-cutoff and 100 pre-cutoff CVEs. Use the vulnerable function before the fix plus its patched version (pairs), and add non-changed functions from the same files to reach a realistic ratio (e.g. 1:20). Manually verify a random 50 positives (two raters, Cohen's κ), as in risse2025top.
58:- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. All tools are free, and a 7B model runs on Colab or a laptop GPU. The hard parts are dataset construction and mapping warnings to functions. Expect 6–10 weeks. A low-cost variant reuses VentiVul from lu2025lab (post-cutoff, data public [@lu2025lab, p. 2]) and adds a SAST arm, an LLM arm with file context, and an all-positive baseline. Run Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep on the whole source files, as deininger2026open did on functions; a CodeQL arm requires building the Linux or Chromium versions, which deininger2026open could not do for snippets [@deininger2026open, p. 10] and which is hard for a beginner.
78:- Confidence: **low–medium**. This is an active area with many 2025–26 preprints. The gap is narrow and could be filled quickly.
79:- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged.** None of the four new papers studies LLM filtering of SAST alarms, and the second-pass cost/triage queries (Q30, Q31) surfaced only items already listed above (arXiv 2607.09979) or non-security triage work. Not re-searched separately.
81:- Suggested study:
82:  - **Data:**
85:  - **Method:** run Semgrep and CodeQL; ask 2 open LLMs (7–8B) for a TP/FP verdict with a confidence score, 3 runs.
93:- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy–moderate**. Ground truth and the scorer are public, Java SAST on OWASP builds easily, and 7B models run locally. Expect 4–6 weeks. The main effort is labelling the real-world alerts.
114:- Confidence: **medium**. Reproductions may exist in artifact-evaluation reports that are not indexed.
115:- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged.** None of the four new papers evaluates IRIS, RepoAudit or another hybrid LLM+SAST detector. Not re-searched separately.
117:- Suggested study:
119:  - **Data:** 30 CWE-Bench-Java CVEs across 4 CWEs, plus 10–15 post-cutoff Java CVEs. IRIS code and data are public [@li2024iris, p. 2].
124:- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate–hard**. Building Java projects for CodeQL and running a hybrid pipeline is demanding. A reduced IRIS-only replication on 20–30 CVEs with an open model is feasible in about 8 weeks. RepoAudit (C/C++, high token cost) is not recommended for a beginner.
128:- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** LLM-only evidence on real WordPress-plugin (PHP) vulnerabilities now exists (Neef et al. 2026, abstract only), and a function-level three-family comparison exists for Python, Java and JavaScript (arXiv 2503.01449, abstract only). What remains open is a comparison of LLMs with *established* SAST tools on real CVEs in PHP and Go, preferably with file or plugin context.
164:- Confidence: **low–medium** (narrowed). Python and JavaScript are being filled quickly, and the Neef et al. full text may turn out to include a tool baseline that its abstract does not mention. The gap is clearest for PHP-with-standard-SAST and for Go.
166:- Suggested study:
172:- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. The tools are free and build-free for PHP and Go, and the PHP labels already exist. The main cost is manual labelling of warnings that fall outside the labelled subset.
176:- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open now reports compute cost (USD) and energy (kJ) per true positive at realistic prevalence for 8 LLMs. What remains open is (a) the human triage term, i.e. analyst time spent on the false positives that come with each true positive, and (b) a quantified cost per true positive for the SAST and fine-tuned DL arms on the same targets.
196:- Confidence: **low–medium** (narrowed). What remains is specific (triage term plus costed non-LLM arms) and fits as a secondary outcome of G2.
198:- Suggested study: measure as a secondary outcome of G2 (same targets). Record compute cost per arm (for SAST and DL: CPU/GPU time × a stated hourly rate, so that they are not left at "≈0"), then time two raters triaging a random 50 warnings per arm. Cost per confirmed TP = (compute + triage minutes × hourly rate) / confirmed TPs, reported with sensitivity bands for hourly rates and at realistic prevalence (e.g. 1:44 as in deininger2026open). Use measured, not FLOP-estimated, energy where possible. Threats: triage time depends on rater skill and on the order in which warnings are shown; API price changes and provider price spread (up to 14× for one model [@deininger2026open, p. 5]).
199:- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. It is cheap if added to G2, but on its own it needs the same infrastructure.
218:- **Second-pass G5 check and the TSARKA web-snippet study**: no new gap; recorded under G1 and G5.
## Dropped or merged candidates

- **Contamination control as a standalone gap (candidate 7)**: *narrowed and merged into G2.* Several LLM-only studies now address it:
  - CWE-Trace (arXiv 2606.20502) reports no measurable contamination advantage on Linux-kernel samples (abstract only);
  - BenchGuard (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-33260-8_22);
  - *Are LLMs Memorizing Bug Benchmarks?* (doi:10.1109/llm4code66737.2025.00005);
  - the ASE 2025 industry paper.

  What remains open is the comparative question (does the LLM advantage over SAST/DL survive post-cutoff?), which G2 tests via pre- vs post-cutoff subsets. Searches: Q19, Q20, W6.
- **Independent labelling, LLM-as-labeller and single runs (W3, W5)**: *merged* into G1 (protocol) and G4 (blinded human labelling). No separate novelty check was run, so they are not reported as separate gaps.
- **Statement-level / location-aware scoring**: *merged* into G1. Evidence: [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8; @gnieciak2025large, p. 6].
- **Workflow / IDE integration**: *not reported.* It is supported by one survey only [@zhou2025large, p. 19], no dedicated three-query novelty check was run, and Q14 surfaced a pilot human study of LLM-augmented SAST reports (doi:10.1109/csr69374.2026.11759919). It needs developer participants and is a poor fit for a beginner.
- **"Does reasoning reduce false positives?" (contradiction C4)**: *not reported as a gap.* tan2026think already provides a controlled factorial test within the corpus [@tan2026think, p. 6], so it is not a gap. deininger2026open adds that the effect is model-dependent: reasoning helps the frontier models but lowers DeepSeek-V3.2's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. The conflicting evidence belongs in the review's discussion, not in this report.
- **Decision threshold and prompt sensitivity (second pass)**: *merged* into G1 (protocol: report threshold choice, several prompts, runs/variance). Evidence: the argmax artefact and prompt-dependent winners in deininger2026open [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. Supported by one paper only and no separate novelty check, so not a separate gap.
- **Label quality of fix-commit benchmarks (second pass)**: *not reported as a new gap.* tashenova2026real finds only 48.8% of cleaned positive labels genuine [@tashenova2026real, p. 11], in line with risse2025top and ding2025vulnerability. This is well documented in the corpus and in the dataset-centric review listed under positioning, so it is a finding for RQ2, not an open gap. It enters G2 and G5 as a threat (verify a labelled sample).
- **Second-pass G5 check and the TSARKA web-snippet study**: no new gap; recorded under G1 and G5.

## Recommended for inclusion (not added; not analysed)

The first-pass recommendations 1–4 (arXiv 2512.10485, doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303, doi:10.3390/computers15090623, doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137) have been added and analysed as lu2025lab, tashenova2026real, deininger2026open and qin2026review, and are removed from this list. The orchestrator decides on the rest. Listed by value to RQ1–RQ3, the gaps and positioning:
1. **arXiv 2503.01449**, Zhang et al. 2025, *Benchmarking Large Language Models for Multi-Language Software Vulnerability Detection* (preprint; check for a published version). **New, high priority.** A second same-benchmark LLM vs fine-tuned small model vs SAST comparison, and the only one in Python, Java and JavaScript. Directly relevant to RQ1, G2 and G5. It was returned by first-pass Q17 but missed.
2. **arXiv 2606.21397**, Neef et al. 2026, *Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection* (AI&CCPS Workshop at ARES 2026, LNCS, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-35576-8_3). **New.** Six LLMs on real WordPress-plugin vulnerabilities, code and data released. It is the closest work to G5 and must be read in full to confirm whether it has a tool baseline and at what granularity it works.
3. **doi:10.5070/sr3.62177**, [SoK] *LLMs in Security Code Review and Testing* (J. Systems Research 2026). Second positioning competitor (LLM vs traditional tools).
4. **arXiv 2604.13764**, *RealVuln* (preprint; authors evaluate their own company's scanner). SAST vs LLM on Python repositories; adds language coverage. Flag the preprint status and conflict of interest.
5. **doi:10.1016/j.infsof.2026.108213**, *Leveraging Large Language Models for advanced static code analysis: Assessing the feasibility of AI superseding traditional vulnerability detection methods* (Information and Software Technology 2026). **New; screen first.** The title suggests an LLM-vs-traditional comparison in a strong venue, but no abstract was retrieved, so its relevance is unknown.
6. **arXiv 2605.23243**, Dahiya et al. 2026, *Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity?* (preprint). **New, low priority.** Frontier vs domain-specialised LLMs on function-level C/Java/Python and black-box web testing; no SAST or DL arm in the abstract. Useful mainly as context for RQ1 (frontier LLM false-positive rates).
7. Optional, for the RQ3 hybrid and filtering discussion: **arXiv 2510.02534** (ZeroFalse) and **arXiv 2610.32876** (*Trusting the Tool*, Oct 2026), both preprints. Optional, for RQ2: **arXiv 2507.21817** (*Out of Distribution, Out of Luck*, ICSE 2026). Optional, for G1 context: **doi:10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11** (TSARKA Science 2026; web snippets, open LLMs vs a rule-based analyser, compares against an all-vulnerable classifier; venue tier unknown).

- Only xiong2026sifting, li2026llm and lu2025lab test on post-cutoff or temporally separated code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5; @lu2025lab, p. 4] [V]; none of the three runs all three families [I].
  - **Survey future work asks only for verified benchmarks.** The surveys' future directions call for verified, contamination-free, repository-level benchmarks [@zhou2025large, p. 22; @sheng2025llms, p. 25] [A], but not for a controlled three-family comparison [I]. deininger2026open plans a post-cutoff restriction [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q6, Q7, Q8 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025, contamination angle Q19, Q20, W3, W6; second pass Q27, Q28, Q29 on OpenAlex/Crossref from 2025, arXiv abstract page A2, W10).
  - **Now in our corpus (analysed):** deininger2026open (three families, function level, pre-cutoff, lightweight SAST), lu2025lab (post-cutoff, no SAST), tashenova2026real (PHP, no LLM). See evidence above.
  - **Dahiya et al. 2026**, *Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity? Evidence for Vertical Foundation Models from Dual-Mode Vulnerability Benchmarks* (arXiv 2605.23243, preprint, v5 June 2026; **abstract only**, A2). Six frontier and two domain-specialised models on (i) white-box *function-level* detection in C/Java/Python built on VulnLLM-R and (ii) black-box testing of five web applications with 118 known vulnerabilities. From the abstract: no SAST baseline (the only tools named are Playwright and Burp Suite MCP servers for black-box testing), no fine-tuned DL detector, no post-cutoff or leakage control mentioned. Its "application-level" track is black-box dynamic testing, not source-code analysis. **Does not fill G2.**
  - **Zhang et al. 2025**, *Benchmarking Large Language Models for Multi-Language Software Vulnerability Detection* (arXiv 2503.01449, preprint; **abstract only**, Q27/W9). Five open LLMs (prompting, instruction tuning, fine-tuning) against five fine-tuned small language models and two open-source SAST tools, on function-level data in Python (8,260 vulnerable functions), Java (7,505) and JavaScript (28,983). Secondary summaries (W9) report that the SAST tools were less effective than both model families. This is a second same-benchmark three-family comparison and the only one outside C/C++ we found. From the abstract: function level, no temporal or post-cutoff separation mentioned, SAST tools not named. It was already returned by first-pass searches (Q17) but was missed in the first version of this report. It narrows the non-C/C++ part of G2 at function level; it does not address post-cutoff code, context or semantic SAST.
  - *Leveraging Large Language Models for advanced static code analysis: Assessing the feasibility of AI superseding traditional vulnerability detection methods* (Information and Software Technology 2026, doi:10.1016/j.infsof.2026.108213; Q32): **title only**, no abstract retrieved (W12). Its scope cannot be judged; it should be screened.
  - *RealVuln* (arXiv 2604.13764): SAST vs LLMs vs specialised scanners on 26 intentionally vulnerable Python repositories. **No DL; not real-world CVEs; the authors' company product is evaluated.**
  - *A Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection: Big-Vul and CVEfixes* (IJANSER 2026, OpenAlex W7218261049): LLMs vs static baselines on balanced Big-Vul/CVEfixes. **No DL; noisy, non-post-cutoff data.**
  - *VulEval* (arXiv 2404.15596, reportedly TSE 2026): repository-level evaluation of DL and LLM methods. From its abstract, no SAST arm.
  - Contamination studies of LLM-only detection, which leave the cross-family comparison open:
    - CWE-Trace (arXiv 2606.20502);
    - BenchGuard (LNCS 2026, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-33260-8_22);
    - the ASE 2025 industry-showcase paper "Should We Evaluate LLM Based Security Analysis Approaches on Open Source Systems" (no identifier returned).

  We found no study that runs semantic SAST, fine-tuned DL and LLMs on the same real-world, de-duplicated, post-cutoff targets with file or repository context and a shared unit and metric (searches on 2026-11-12). Function-level, pre-cutoff three-family comparisons do exist (deininger2026open for C/C++; arXiv 2503.01449 for Python/Java/JS, abstract only).
- Confidence: **medium** (narrowed). The remaining gap is more specific, so it is easier to defend, but near misses now lack only one or two conditions (post-cutoff, context, semantic SAST). Re-check before submission.
- Potential contribution: the first like-for-like answer to RQ1 on realistic, post-cutoff code, and an estimate of how much of the LLM advantage is due to contamination (pre- vs post-cutoff subsets; deininger2026open already finds a recall gradient by CVE year [@deininger2026open, p. 24]). It would also test whether deininger's metric-dependent ranking (DL best on balanced accuracy, SAST best on precision) survives with context and semantic SAST. This also absorbs candidate gap 7 (contamination).
- Suggested study:
  - **Data:** Python (build-free for SAST) or Java CVEs. Collect vulnerability-fixing commits from GitHub Security Advisories/OSV (CVEfixes or MoreFixes pipeline). Split into a *post-cutoff* set (disclosed after the newest evaluated model's training cutoff) and a *pre-cutoff* set of the same size.
  - **Sample:** about 100 post-cutoff and 100 pre-cutoff CVEs. Use the vulnerable function before the fix plus its patched version (pairs), and add non-changed functions from the same files to reach a realistic ratio (e.g. 1:20). Manually verify a random 50 positives (two raters, Cohen's κ), as in risse2025top.
  - **Arms:**
    - SAST: Semgrep (security rulesets) and CodeQL `security-extended`, default and tuned query suites.
    - DL: UniXcoder or CodeBERT fine-tuned on pre-cutoff data with project-disjoint splits.
    - LLM: 2–3 open 7–14B models (local) and optionally one API model, zero-shot and chain-of-thought, 3 runs each.
  - **Unit mapping:** a SAST warning counts for the function that contains its line. Also report file-level results so that SAST is not penalised by the mapping.
  - **Metrics:** recall, precision and MCC at the natural ratio; pairwise correctness on pairs; flag rate; cost (USD, GPU-hours, wall time).
  - **Baselines:** flag-all, random, and a function-length classifier (competitive in tashenova2026real [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]).
  - **Analysis:** McNemar tests between arms on identical functions; project-level bootstrap CIs; pre- vs post-cutoff difference per arm as a contamination estimate.
  - **Threats:**
    - noisy fix-commit labels;
    - function mapping disadvantages SAST;
    - small fine-tuning data for Python;
    - prompt sensitivity;
    - residual contamination (advisories published before the CVE date);
    - limited generalisation beyond one language.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. All tools are free, and a 7B model runs on Colab or a laptop GPU. The hard parts are dataset construction and mapping warnings to functions. Expect 6–10 weeks. A low-cost variant reuses VentiVul from lu2025lab (post-cutoff, data public [@lu2025lab, p. 2]) and adds a SAST arm, an LLM arm with file context, and an all-positive baseline. Run Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep on the whole source files, as deininger2026open did on functions; a CodeQL arm requires building the Linux or Chromium versions, which deininger2026open could not do for snippets [@deininger2026open, p. 10] and which is hard for a beginner.

## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
- Gap type: practical / methodological
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **xiong2026sifting.** The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
    - The miss rate is low for injection CWEs (CWE-78 2.38%, CWE-89 1.10%, CWE-79 0.41%) [V].
    - It is 77.17% for weak cryptography and 84.50% for weak hashing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
    - The authors plan "CWE-aware, cost-adaptive agent strategies and human-in-the-loop" auditing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A].
## G5: Real-CVE LLM-vs-standard-SAST evidence is missing for PHP and Go (JavaScript and Python only partly covered)
- Gap type: population/context
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** LLM-only evidence on real WordPress-plugin (PHP) vulnerabilities now exists (Neef et al. 2026, abstract only), and a function-level three-family comparison exists for Python, Java and JavaScript (arXiv 2503.01449, abstract only). What remains open is a comparison of LLMs with *established* SAST tools on real CVEs in PHP and Go, preferably with file or plugin context.
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **The literature is concentrated on C/C++ and Java.**
    - Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28] [V].
    - 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34] [V].
    - Directions call for Python, Java, Rust and multilingual benchmarks [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 40] [A].
  - **Authors list other languages as future work:**
    - RepoAudit: extension to Python and JavaScript [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 10] [A];
    - IRIS: other languages [@li2024iris, p. 10] [A];
    - du2026reducing: more languages [@du2026reducing, p. 10] [A];
    - xiong2026sifting: more languages and SAST tools [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A];
    - li2026llm: broader languages and CWE classes [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A];
    - deininger2026open: other languages [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
    - lu2025lab: VentiVul is C/C++ only and may not generalise to other languages [@lu2025lab, p. 17] [A].
  - **The few multi-language studies are thin or lack SAST.**
    - The multi-language LLM study in our corpus (REEF, 7 languages) has no SAST arm [@shu2026evaluating, p. 7] [V].
    - zhou2024comparison covers Python with roughly 8–10 test CVEs per language [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
  - **The only PHP study in our corpus has no LLM and no standard SAST tool.** tashenova2026real builds a real-CVE WordPress-plugin benchmark (1757 CVEs, 1281 plugins) [@tashenova2026real, p. 3] [V]. Its SAST arm is an unnamed, in-house, intra-procedural lexical taint analyser [@tashenova2026real, p. 5; @tashenova2026real, p. 13] [V] that detects only 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities [@tashenova2026real, p. 9] [V]. The authors attribute the low recall to "that implementation rather than taint analysis in general" [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A]. No LLM or transformer was run [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [V]. Its "misses about 98%" result therefore says nothing about established PHP SAST tools or about LLMs [I]. It works at function level, not plugin or repository level [I].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q17, Q18, Q26 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025 and W8; second pass Q32 on OpenAlex/Crossref, Q33 on OpenAlex, Q34 on arXiv, all from 2025, arXiv abstract page A1, W9). Closest hits:
  - **Neef et al. 2026**, *Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection* (arXiv 2606.21397, v1 19 June 2026; to appear at the AI&CCPS Workshop at ARES 2026, LNCS, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-35576-8_3; **abstract only**, A1, Q32, Q34). Cited by deininger2026open as comparing open and frontier LLMs on WordPress-plugin web vulnerability detection [@deininger2026open, p. 3]. From the abstract:
    - six frontier and open-weight LLMs; real-world WordPress-plugin vulnerabilities (SQL injection, stored XSS, path traversal, RCE); five prompt designs; three iterations;
    - best detection rate 63% (Claude Opus 4.6), 48% for open-weight MiniMax M2.5, 35% for self-hosted Qwen 3.5; scoped prompts beat open-ended ones; no model was fully consistent across iterations; code and data are published;
    - **no SAST tool baseline** is named (the LLMs themselves perform "static analysis"); no fine-tuned DL detector; the number of plugins or CVEs and the input granularity (function, file or whole plugin) are not stated in the abstract; PHP is not named explicitly, but WordPress plugins are PHP code [I].
    - **Effect on G5:** it fills the "LLMs on real PHP CVEs" part, so G5 is **narrowed**. It does not fill the LLM-vs-SAST comparison. Whether it works at plugin (repository) level must be checked in the full text.
  - **Zhang et al. 2025** (arXiv 2503.01449, preprint; abstract only; see G2): function-level Python, Java and JavaScript, LLMs vs fine-tuned small models vs two open-source SAST tools. It covers JavaScript and Python at function level, not repository level.
  - *On-premise open-weight LLMs for interpretable web vulnerability detection* (TSARKA Science 2026, doi:10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11; abstract only, Q32): 120 annotated web-application snippets, five open models vs a rule-based static analyser and published cloud-model results. Snippet level, not real CVEs at repository level; venue tier unknown.
  - *Benchmarking Static Analysis for PHP Applications Security* (Entropy 2025, doi:10.3390/e27090926; abstract only, Q32): an evaluation framework for PHP SAST tools; no LLM.
  - *RealVuln* (arXiv 2604.13764): Python, but intentionally vulnerable repositories and a vendor author.
  - JavaScript:
    - *LLMs Cannot Reliably Detect Vulnerabilities in JavaScript* (arXiv 2512.01255): LLM-focused benchmark;
    - *Exploring Automated Vulnerability Identification in JavaScript Code Using LLMs* (arXiv 2609.13816): snippet-level, LLM vs SAST.
  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): LLMs only, C/C++/Python.
  - *A Preliminary Study of LLMs for Multilingual Vulnerability Detection* (ISSTA companion 2025, doi:10.1145/3713081.3731746): PLMs vs LLMs, no SAST.
  - Go: Q33 returned no Go-specific LLM-vs-SAST study.

  We found no study comparing LLMs with an established SAST tool on real CVEs for PHP or Go, and only function-level, snippet-level or synthetic-repository LLM-vs-SAST evidence for JavaScript and Python (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **low–medium** (narrowed). Python and JavaScript are being filled quickly, and the Neef et al. full text may turn out to include a tool baseline that its abstract does not mention. The gap is clearest for PHP-with-standard-SAST and for Go.
- Potential contribution: tests whether the "LLM higher recall, lower precision" pattern holds in web languages, where injection CWEs (which LLMs handle best [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]) dominate.
- Suggested study:
  - **Data (PHP):** the expert-verified subset released with tashenova2026real, 125 vulnerable and 247 safe functions [@tashenova2026real, p. 11], plus the corresponding plugin versions (reconstructed from WordPress.org with the released loader [@tashenova2026real, p. 14]) for file-level runs. If Neef et al. 2026 released their plugin set (its abstract says code and data are published), reuse it so the LLM results can be compared with theirs. **Data (Go):** about 60 Go CVEs from the Go vulnerability database (OSV).
  - **Arms:** established SAST (Semgrep with PHP or Go rules; for PHP also a taint-mode tool such as Psalm or Progpilot; for Go, gosec), 2 open LLMs at function level and at file level with retrieved callers, the token-count baseline from tashenova2026real [@tashenova2026real, p. 8], and flag-all. Check CodeQL's supported-language list for the chosen language before planning a CodeQL arm.
  - **Metrics:** recall on known CVEs; precision on a manually labelled warning sample; cost.
  - **Analysis:** per-CWE recall with CIs.
  - **Threats:** label quality (tashenova2026real finds only 48.8% of cleaned positive labels genuine, single annotator [@tashenova2026real, p. 11]; using its expert-verified subset reduces this); small samples (125 positives give wide CIs; report Wilson intervals); tool coverage differences (some CWE classes are outside a tool's rules); old plugin versions may no longer be downloadable (about 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable in tashenova2026real [@tashenova2026real, p. 3]); contamination (pre-2025 CVEs are likely in LLM pre-training data).
- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. The tools are free and build-free for PHP and Go, and the PHP labels already exist. The main cost is manual labelling of warnings that fall outside the labelled subset.

## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison that includes human triage effort and a costed SAST and DL arm on the same targets
- Gap type: practical
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open now reports compute cost (USD) and energy (kJ) per true positive at realistic prevalence for 8 LLMs. What remains open is (a) the human triage term, i.e. analyst time spent on the false positives that come with each true positive, and (b) a quantified cost per true positive for the SAST and fine-tuned DL arms on the same targets.

content.content:
**3.4 CodeQL on CWE-Bench-Java (partly comparable).** CodeQL detects 27 of 120 CVEs (22.5%) in the IRIS paper [@li2024iris, p. 8] and has 14.19% recall on li2026llm's Java set [@li2026llm, p. 9]. That set mixes a Maven-only CWE-Bench-Java subset with 50 JLeaks resource leaks [@li2026llm, p. 5]. [I] Both values are low, and the gap is plausibly due to the different CWE mix and CodeQL versions.

**3.5 LLM-vs-SAST headline numbers (not comparable).** gnieciak counts LLM findings as true positives even when the line or column is wrong, which SAST tools are not allowed [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. dubniczky uses a severity-weighted score [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 10]. khare uses function-level accuracy on balanced sets [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. zhou2024 uses CVE detection ratio and marked-function ratio [@zhou2024comparison, p. 5]. li2026llm uses recall on known CVEs and SFDR on new code [@li2026llm, p. 11]. deininger2026open scores LLMs and SAST on identical functions with identical metrics (balanced accuracy and precision at 1:44) [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. Within that one study, the comparison is like-for-like. Its SAST arm is lightweight, though: Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep, with no CodeQL [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] These six studies cannot be pooled or ranked against each other. tashenova2026real reports macro-F1 on PHP for a bespoke analyser [@tashenova2026real, p. 8] and does not add to this comparison.

**3.6 False-positive filtering (not numerically comparable).** du measures removal of false alarms on 433 industrial alarms of general bug types [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. xiong measures residual FPR and TP miss rate on OWASP and 100 sampled alerts [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. Only the qualitative pattern can be compared (§3.9, G7).

**3.7 Unpaired PrimeVul functions vs PrimeVul pairs (not comparable; do not pool).** The two designs differ as follows:
- **deininger** samples 1549 single functions (35.4% vulnerable) from the PrimeVul test split [@deininger2026open, p. 4]. It reports balanced accuracy 0.511–0.711 for LLMs and 0.765 for fine-tuned CodeBERT [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **ding, tan and yildiz** score both members of each vulnerable/patched pair together (§3.2).

The unit, prevalence and metric all differ. [I] Balanced accuracy on single functions and pair-wise correctness answer different questions. The first asks whether a detector ranks vulnerable functions above safe ones. The second asks whether it notices the fix. So "fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all LLMs" (deininger) and "GPT-4 beats fine-tuned models on pairs" (ding) are not a numerical contradiction; C1 discusses them. Even inside one study, yildiz's F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. deininger's PrimeVul test split (24,788 functions, 549 vulnerable) also differs from the split recorded by ding (695 vulnerable / 25,216 benign) [@deininger2026open, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. deininger explains this only as "after loading".

**3.8 Detection at realistic prevalence (not numerically comparable; same direction).** Two studies score detectors at about 2% prevalence against a trivial baseline:
- **deininger** (PrimeVul, 1:44 ≈ 2.2%): every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% in the first epoch and 2.8–4.6% in the budget-matched epoch, vs 2.21% for flag-all [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **lu** (VentiVul, 1.97% [I]): trained DL reaches F1 3.47–8.65, and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14].

The datasets, metrics (precision vs F1) and models differ (frontier and open LLMs vs open LLMs ≤ 32B). [I] Both show LLMs only slightly above, or below, a classifier that flags everything.

- yildiz shows the same sensitivity: F1 falls from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- Pass 2 adds two more cases:
  - deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8].
  - In tashenova, changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
- [I] Explanation: LLMs flag positives more liberally, which balanced sets reward. Rankings from balanced benchmarks should not be carried over to deployment, where vulnerable code is rare.

**C6. Hybrid IRIS: original vs independent evaluation.**
- Claim A: IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27 detected; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8].
- Claim B: on 15 real-world Java projects, IRIS (GPT-4) has 97.80% SFDR vs 77.00% for CodeQL [@li2026llm, p. 12].
- Differences: known CVEs vs new code, detections vs SFDR, CodeQL-protocol FDR vs Codex-labelled sampling.
- [I] Explanation: hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen projects. The comparison is not like-for-like, so the tension stays open.

**C7. Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score: lu2025lab vs ding2025vulnerability.**
- Claim A: LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul reaches F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12].
- Claim B: CodeBERT trained and tested on BigVul reaches F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- Differences: neither paper explains the 28-point gap. lu used LineVul's original pipeline and recommended settings [@lu2025lab, p. 8], whereas ding trains its own set of code LMs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- [I] Explanation: likely split and preprocessing differences. In-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers (§3.3).

**C8. Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive? deininger2026open vs lu2025lab.**
- Claim A: CodeBERT-PrimeVul keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split [@deininger2026open, p. 3; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. At 1:44 prevalence this corresponds to F1 ≈ 0.15 (our calculation from reported TPR and precision).
- Claim B: DL trained on BigVul, ICVul, Devign or Juliet falls to F1 3.47–8.65 on post-May-2025 VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 13].
- Differences:
  - test data: PrimeVul functions with CVEs from 2008–2022 [@deininger2026open, p. 24] vs VentiVul 2025 CVEs scored per function across whole files [@lu2025lab, p. 4];
  - training data: PrimeVul's own training split vs older, noisier benchmarks;
  - threshold policy: validation-tuned [@deininger2026open, p. 11] vs the original implementations' settings [@lu2025lab, p. 8];
  - metric: balanced accuracy vs F1.
- [I] Explanation: unresolved. A detector trained on cleaner data from the same source, with a tuned threshold, may hold up better than detectors trained on other benchmarks. Neither study tests this directly.

## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field

- **W1. Trivial baselines rarely reported.** On a 50/50 set, "flag everything" scores F1 0.667, so balanced-data F1 near that value shows no skill. Examples:
  - shu's DummyClf_vul scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - tan's best F1 is 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7; @tan2026think, p. 11].
  - All of yildiz's GPT F1 values (48–66) are at or below it [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - khare's best-per-dataset F1s include always-vulnerable rows [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].

  Pass 2 shows the same problem at other prevalences (G10):
  - deininger: the best LLM F1 (0.615) is 0.092 above always-vulnerable (0.523), and Qwen3-Coder-30B (0.405) is below it [@deininger2026open, p. 7].
  - tashenova: a token-count baseline is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
  - lu reports no trivial baseline. [I] By our calculation, 7 of its 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 14].

  [I] Only shu, deininger and tashenova report trivial-classifier baselines (3 of 19 primary studies). ding reports a random reference only for pair-wise correctness [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. tashenova's authors argue that detectors should be required to clear such baselines [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A].
- **W2. Label quality and leakage.** Problems include:
  - **Exact-copy leakage** from test to train reaches 12.7% (BigVul) and 18.9% (CVEFixes) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Even plugin-grouped PHP folds contained duplicate groups spanning folds (166 / 151 groups) and 730 / 456 groups with contradictory labels before cleaning [@tashenova2026real, p. 4].
  - **Label quality** is low wherever it is audited: 39–65% [@risse2025top, p. 8], 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] and 48.8% for PHP [@tashenova2026real, p. 11] of positive labels are correct. [I] tashenova's evaluated corpus also contains lower-tier labels, so its true label precision is probably lower still. Its authors argue that label quality, not architecture, is "the more plausible binding constraint" [@tashenova2026real, p. 12] [A].
  - **Contamination.** Benchmarks probably sit in LLM pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A]. deininger finds recall 7–15 points higher on pre-2020 than on 2021–2022 CVEs for better-balanced LLMs, which is consistent with memorisation [@deininger2026open, p. 24].
  - **Post-cutoff testing** is rare. Only xiong, li2026llm and lu test explicitly on code disclosed after the evaluated models' release [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5; @lu2025lab, p. 5]. lu notes that release-date separation cannot fully exclude contamination [@lu2025lab, p. 17]. shu adds a time split [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
- **W3. LLM-as-labeller.** li2026llm labels real-world warnings with Codex, a tool it also evaluates (94.36% accurate on 621 validated warnings) [@li2026llm, p. 11]. tan's LLM judge rates explanations higher in ways humans corroborate only for informativeness [@tan2026think, p. 8]. [I] Self-labelling can favour the labelling model.
- **W4. Unequal scoring between LLMs and SAST.** gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. CASTLE's LLM prompt states the reward and penalty scheme [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]. SAST tools run on default configurations [@gnieciak2025large, p. 8], and khare tests CodeQL only on synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]. [I] These choices favour LLMs in two studies and SAST in one.
- **W5. Single runs, no statistics.** Most studies report one run of non-deterministic models without variance (§1). Examples:
  - zhou2024's results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs per language [I] [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6].
  - xiong's real-world samples are 50 alerts each [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13].
  - shu chooses the best of ~30 configurations post hoc [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - lu runs each LLM once and does not report DL run counts [@lu2025lab, p. 8].
  - tashenova uses a single seed [@tashenova2026real, p. 7].

  deininger shows why this matters. A reworded prompt moves balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and changes which model wins [@deininger2026open, p. 19; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. Absolute scores shift by up to 0.06 between measurement epochs seven weeks apart [@deininger2026open, p. 20].
- **W6. Little cost reporting; energy figures of mixed provenance.** Twelve of 19 primary studies report no monetary cost (§1). Where cost is measured it is decisive: up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Only deininger reports cost per true positive (G11), and it excludes human triage [@deininger2026open, p. 8]. Its energy figures mix three sources:
  - Frontier-model energy is a FLOP estimate that assumes 100B active parameters [@deininger2026open, p. 7].
  - The kJ per TP for Gemma, Qwen and Llama come from FLOP estimates (64, 40 and 944 J per task), not from measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 14].
  - The FLOP estimator overstates measured batched energy by 5.4–16.9× [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

  [I] With measured single-request energy, our recalculation gives about 4.9 (Gemma), 8.8 (Qwen) and 34.9 (Llama) kJ per TP. The ordering among open models changes, but the gap to frontier models remains. Energy numbers should always state whether they are measured or estimated.
- **W7. Narrow scope.** Data are C/C++-biased and long-tailed, and 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34]. 87 studies build custom datasets and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. Only one of 40 detection studies to March 2024 worked at repository level [@zhou2025large, p. 18]. PHP is covered by a single function-level study, which has no LLM arm and only a bespoke analyser [@tashenova2026real, p. 13].
- **W8. Three-way comparisons are rare.** [I] Two studies evaluate LLMs, SAST and DL together:
  - khare, whose SAST arm covers synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7];
  - deininger, on identical PrimeVul functions with lightweight SAST and no CodeQL [@deininger2026open, p. 10], using CVEs from 2008–2022 that predate the models' training cutoffs [@deininger2026open, p. 24].

  zhou2024 compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST but no classic DL detector [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4]. lu compares DL with LLMs but has no SAST arm, and tashenova compares SAST with ML/DL but has no LLM arm [@lu2025lab, p. 7; @tashenova2026real, p. 13].
- **W9. Preprint text vs version of record.** Fifteen published papers were analysed from arXiv copies (xiong2026sifting's copy is the formatted published article). lu2025lab was read as the arXiv v4 accepted manuscript of its JSS 2026 version [@lu2025lab, p. 1]. du2026reducing comes from a v1 with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2], so it has the highest risk that numbers changed. zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own zhou2024comparison [@zhou2025large, p. 22], so it is not independent support.
- **W10. Independence.** [I] Several sources overlap:
  - guo and li2026llm share five C/C++ modules.
  - ding, yildiz, tan and deininger all draw on PrimeVul.
  - Duplication figures reused elsewhere trace back to ding alone (critical review B).
  - qin2026review's quantitative claims re-report ding and gnieciak, so they add no independent support [@qin2026review, p. 12].
  - ICVul, one of lu's four training benchmarks, is the authors' own dataset [@lu2025lab, p. 3].
- **W11. Test prevalence rarely realistic.** Most test sets are balanced or close to it (W1), while vulnerable code is rare in practice. The pass-2 studies show what this hides:
  - Re-scored at PrimeVul's natural 1:44 ratio, LLMs raise 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8].
  - At BigVul's 6% prevalence, DL accuracy of 87–94% hides F1 as low as 0.19 [@lu2025lab, p. 11].
  - tashenova draws negatives only from vulnerable plugins [@tashenova2026real, p. 3]. [I] Its prevalence is therefore 74.5% (Variant A) and 46.2% (Variant B), and the false-alarm rate in deployment is unknown.

  [I] Results from balanced sets should be re-scored at realistic prevalence before any deployment claim.

## 6. What this means for our research questions

Updated pass 2, 2026-11-12 (24 papers). The same answers appear in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

**RQ1 — effectiveness head-to-head.** No family wins across settings.
- **LLMs vs SAST.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale, general coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) [@li2026llm, p. 7], but most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 11].
- **Same functions, all three families.** On 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions, seven of eight zero-shot LLMs beat lightweight SAST on balanced accuracy [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence, though, Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM. LLM precision there (2.3–4.6%) is barely above flag-all (2.21%) [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **LLMs vs fine-tuned DL.** The ranking depends on dataset, class balance and decision threshold [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. A fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all eight LLMs on the same unpaired PrimeVul functions (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]. All families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].
