## 1. Research objective
- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (demonstrations drawn from complete vulnerable–patched pairs, the same number from each project; k = 4 is given only "for example", and the k actually used is not stated), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] Each of the 263 pairs has exactly one vulnerable function (p. 4), so prevalence p = 263/13,326 = 1.97%. The Table 7 numbers confirm this: back-calculating prevalence from accuracy, precision and recall gives 1.97% for every LineVul row, which matches 263/13,326. The ReVeal rows give 1.79%, because ReVeal is scored only on the functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). An all-positive classifier would therefore score F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87% on the full set and ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset (our calculation from p. 4 and Table 7 p. 13).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests or confidence intervals. LLMs use one deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8). For DL training, the number of runs and the random seeds are not reported (p. 8 refers only to the original authors' "recommended settings").

## 7. Key findings
1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). [A] Because BigVul has a much smaller vulnerable share (6%), "predictions biased toward the non-vulnerable majority class can produce high accuracy while detecting few vulnerable functions" (p. 11).
2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
5. DL vs LLM on VentiVul (mostly but not exactly the same samples) [V/I] — [V] best DL Whole-File F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [V] The evaluated samples differ: ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), the few-shot test set excludes pairs used as demonstrations, and valid-only metrics use only parseable outputs (p. 8). [I] F1 against chance (all-positive F1 ≈ 3.87% at p = 1.97%; ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset; §4): the best DL F1 of 8.65 is about 2.5× its chance level, while the best LLM F1 of 5.36 is about 1.4× chance. LineVul (Devign), with recall 100%, precision 2% and F1 3.93, is in effect the all-positive predictor (p. 13, Table 7). [I] PACC against chance: a random labeller that flags a fraction q of functions independently of their content would get PACC = q(1−q), up to 25% at q = 0.5. All observed PACC values (≤ 5.75%, DL and LLM) are far below that, which means the models usually give the vulnerable and the patched version the same label (our reasoning from the PACC definition, p. 9). This matches ding2025vulnerability, where random pair-wise correctness is 22.70% and models fall far below it [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). The LLM project-specific results are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
## 1. Research objective
[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), stating "We make no claim to be first on any single one of these axes" (p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
- [I] Implicit questions:
  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
- Baselines or comparison conditions:
  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
  - [V] **DL arm:**
    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
  - [I] This differs from the PrimeVul test split recorded in ding2025vulnerability (695 vulnerable / 25,216 benign) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. The paper does not explain the difference beyond "after loading" (p. 4); filtering or de-duplication on load is plausible but not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method:
  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones (p. 4).
  - [A] "The two non-LLM baselines" see the untruncated function and are therefore "if anything, advantaged" on long inputs (p. 4). [V] But the CodeBERT-Devign baseline uses "inputs truncated to 512 tokens" (p. 6); the input length of CodeBERT-PrimeVul is not reported (pp. 10–11).
  - [I] The untruncated claim can hold only for the SAST tools. CodeBERT's 512-token window is shorter than the LLMs' 8000-character budget, so on long functions CodeBERT is, if anything, disadvantaged — which strengthens rather than weakens its win over the LLMs (basis: p. 4, p. 6; CodeBERT-PrimeVul's limit inferred from the architecture, not reported).
  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
## 7. Key findings
1. **Detection quality, first epoch** — [V] Balanced accuracy / F1 per model, direct mode, N = 1549 (p. 7, Table 4). [V] F1 range across LLMs is 0.405–0.615 vs always-vulnerable F1 0.523 (p. 7, Table 4).

   | Model | Bal. acc. (95% CI) | F1 |
   |---|---|---|

2. **Open vs frontier significance** — [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 significantly beats all three frontier models: +0.054 to +0.060 balanced accuracy, Holm p < 5×10⁻⁴ (p. 6, p. 27, Table A1).
   - [V] Gemma-3-4B beats Claude-Sonnet-5 (+0.037, Holm p = 0.032); the other top-open gaps are not significant (p. 7, p. 27).
   - [V] Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance (MCC 0.022, CI −0.03 to 0.07) (p. 7).
3. **Budget-matched second epoch (Family A)** — [V] Balanced accuracy / MCC: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.711 / 0.403; GLM-5 0.669 / 0.352; Gemma-3-4B 0.653 / 0.297; Claude-Sonnet-5 0.653 / 0.321; GPT-5.1 0.615 / 0.225; Llama 0.609 / 0.267; Qwen 0.568 / 0.136; Gemini 0.606 / 0.252, on only the 54.2% of tasks it answered (p. 17, Table 11).
   - [V] Claude equals Gemma (+0.0003, p = 0.98) (p. 17).
   - [V] Absolute numbers shifted by up to 0.06 between epochs seven weeks apart ("service drift") (p. 7–8, p. 20).

   - [V] Best observed: DeepSeek 0.711 (direct) vs Claude 0.685 and Gemini 0.680 (reasoning); DeepSeek vs Claude p = 0.081 (p. 17).
   - [V] Reasoning lowers DeepSeek's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 (p. 20).
5. **Prompt sensitivity dominates** — [V] Two paraphrases move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and produce three different winners (DeepSeek 0.711, Claude 0.741, GLM-5 0.700); Spearman ρ vs anchor = 0.381 and 0.810 (p. 19–20, Table 13).

# Research report: LLM-based vs traditional static analysis and deep learning for source-code vulnerability detection

- Project: `2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis`
- Date: 2026-11-12
- Based on: 20 full-text analyses, `evidence-matrix.md`, `reports/methodology-comparison.md`, `gap-report.md`, two critical reviews (A and B, 2026-11-12), `search/screening.md`, `search/search-log.md`.
- How to read the labels: **[V]** means we checked the number in the paper's own tables or results, **[A]** means the authors say it but we cannot check it, and **[I]** is our own interpretation. Unlabelled numbers are [V] from the cited page. Citations give the paper's folder name and the PDF page, e.g. `[@risse2025top, p. 8]`.

## 1. Summary in plain language

We asked whether large language models (LLMs, such as GPT-4 or Claude) find security bugs in source code better than the two older approaches: rule-based scanners (SAST tools such as CodeQL) and neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code (deep-learning or "DL" detectors). The short answer is that **no approach wins everywhere**. LLMs come out ahead on small, self-contained programs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL comes out ahead on synthetic test suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. On large real projects both families miss many bugs and raise many false alarms [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. The most consistent pattern [I] is that LLMs find more of the real bugs (higher recall) but also flag much more harmless code (lower precision). A large part of the disagreement between papers comes from **how** they test, not from the tools themselves. Studies differ in label quality, overlap between training and test data, the share of vulnerable samples, and how lenient the scoring is [@risse2025top, p. 8; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. Combining the two, by letting an LLM filter a scanner's alarms, removes most false alarms cheaply but also throws away 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. For your comparative review, this "setup explains the contradictions" angle, applied across all three families, is the contribution we could not find in existing reviews (medium confidence).

Every search is logged in `search/search-log.md`, and every screening decision with its reason is in `search/screening.md`.
- **Two passes.** Pass 1 analysed 20 papers. The pass-1 gap check found four papers that bore directly on our gaps and on the positioning of the review; with your approval they were added in pass 2.
- **Included papers.** 24 papers in total: 20 primary studies and 4 reviews (kaniewski2026systematic, zhou2025large, sheng2025llms and qin2026review). `rlab status` counts 4 of the 24 as preprints:
  - IRIS [@li2024iris, p. 1] and RepoAudit [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 1] appeared at ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025. Both are peer-reviewed, but `rlab` records them as arXiv preprints because those venues issue no DOIs.
  - lu2025lab is recorded as an arXiv preprint, but it is published in the *Journal of Systems and Software* (2026, doi:10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185), so we treat it as peer-reviewed. We read the arXiv v4 accepted manuscript, and its page references follow that version [@lu2025lab, p. 1].
  - Only zhou2024comparison is a true preprint, meaning it is **not peer-reviewed** [@zhou2024comparison, p. 1].
  - qin2026review is published, but in a low-visibility venue that does not document peer review [@qin2026review, p. 1]. It is a weak narrative review (single author, no search protocol), so we give it the weight of *grey literature* (material outside the normal peer-reviewed channels) and use it only to position our review.
  - One pass-1 candidate (VulnLLM-R) was dropped to keep to the 20-paper target, because it is a preprint with no venue.
- **Full text.** 24 of 24 papers were read in full and none were abstract-only (`rlab status`).
  - Pass 1: 18 PDFs were fetched automatically from legal open-access sources, SecVulEval came from its arXiv preprint, and tan2026think came from a publisher PDF that you supplied.
  - Pass 2: lu2025lab and qin2026review were fetched automatically. tashenova2026real and deininger2026open are open access, but the publisher blocked automated download, so you supplied the PDFs.
  - 15 published papers, plus lu2025lab, were read from their arXiv versions, not the publisher's final text (the *version of record*). Numbers could differ slightly between the two (see §7).
- **Quality control.** Four independent critical reviews checked every analysis against the paper text.
  - Pass 1 (reviews A and B): 36 findings, all fixed. Most were small: labels, wording, or relative vs absolute percentages. None changed a paper's headline result.
  - Pass 2 (reviews C and D): 9 findings for qin2026review, 16 for lu2025lab, 10 plus minor notes for tashenova2026real and 12 for deininger2026open, all fixed. Several were substantive, e.g. separating measured from estimated energy figures and limiting tashenova2026real's "SAST misses ~98%" result to the authors' own in-house analyser.
- **Gap checks.** Before any gap was claimed we ran targeted novelty searches, as our standards require (`gap-report.md`): 26 searches and 8 web searches in pass 1, and 9 more searches (Q27–Q35), 4 web searches and 2 directly read arXiv abstract pages in pass 2, all on 2026-11-12. The arXiv service timed out on 6 of the pass-2 searches (see §7).

**Answer.** It depends on the setting:
- **Small, self-contained code.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on ten C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10], and a CASTLE score of 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- **Synthetic suites.** CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **Whole projects.** General coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST on C/C++ (59.55% vs 0–34.29%). Most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- **Against fine-tuned DL.** The ranking depends on the dataset and on the share of vulnerable samples [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. On PrimeVul pairs of vulnerable and fixed code, every family scores near or below chance [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].

**Evidence strength: weak to moderate.** The studies are mostly single runs, use five incompatible headline metrics, and cannot be pooled [I] (methodology comparison §3.5).

**What would change it.** A study that runs all three families on the same real, recent code with one shared metric (gap G2). Only khare2025understanding runs all three, and its SAST arm is on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7].

**Answer.** It depends on the setting and on which score you use:
- **Small, self-contained code.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on ten C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10], and a CASTLE score of 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- **Synthetic suites.** CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **Whole projects.** General coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST on C/C++ (59.55% vs 0–34.29%). Most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- **All three families on the same real functions (new in pass 2).** deininger2026open tests 8 LLMs, 3 lightweight SAST tools and fine-tuned CodeBERT detectors on the same 1549 C/C++ functions from the PrimeVul dataset.
  - Seven of the eight LLMs, asked without examples (*zero-shot*), beat the SAST tools on *balanced accuracy*, a score that averages how well a tool handles vulnerable and safe code [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10].
  - A fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all eight LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
  - When the functions are re-scored at the dataset's natural mix (about 1 vulnerable function for every 44 safe ones, "1:44"), Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM. LLM precision is 2.3–4.6%, barely above the 2.21% of a rule that flags everything [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **Against fine-tuned DL elsewhere.** The ranking depends on the dataset, the share of vulnerable samples and the *decision threshold* (the score above which a model says "vulnerable") [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. On PrimeVul pairs of vulnerable and fixed code, every family scores near or below chance [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].
- **Recent code (new in pass 2).** On Linux and Chromium vulnerabilities disclosed from May 2025, where 1.97% of functions are vulnerable, trained DL detectors reach F1 3.47–8.65 and four open LLMs of up to 32B parameters reach 0.79–5.36 [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. By our calculation, a rule that flags everything would score about 3.87, so both families sit close to it [I].
- **PHP (new in pass 2).** No LLM has been tested on PHP in our corpus. The authors' own in-house analyser detects only 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins [@tashenova2026real, p. 9], which says nothing about established PHP SAST tools [I].

**Evidence strength: weak to moderate.** The studies are mostly single runs, use incompatible headline metrics, and cannot be pooled [I] (methodology comparison §3.5). Only one study compares all three families on identical real functions, and its SAST arm is lightweight: CodeQL could not be run on isolated functions [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. The most robust pattern [I] is that LLMs have higher recall and lower precision, and that at realistic prevalence their margin over trivial baselines is small.

**What would change it.** A study that runs all three families, including a *semantic* SAST tool such as CodeQL, on the same real code released after the models' training cutoff, with file or repository context and one shared metric (gap G2). khare2025understanding runs all three, but its SAST arm is on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]; deininger2026open uses pre-2023 CVEs and single functions [@deininger2026open, p. 24]. A preprint comparing LLMs, fine-tuned small models and SAST in Python, Java and JavaScript (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv 2503.01449; abstract only, not analysed) could extend the answer beyond C/C++ if added (§8).

**Answer.** Yes, to a large extent. The main sources of variation are:
- **Wrong labels.** Only 39–65% of "vulnerable" labels in popular datasets are correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- **Test data copied from training data.** Up to 18.9% exact copies [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4].
- **Balanced vs realistic test sets.** The class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. LLM F1 falls from about 49–65% to 5.41–12.21% when pairs are dropped [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- **Synthetic vs real code.** LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
- **Function-level vs line-level scoring.** Line-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
- **Custom datasets with inconsistent splits** [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Even a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11], so high scores on that dataset say little about real understanding.

**Evidence strength: moderate to strong.** Independent primary studies agree, and two systematic reviews concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].

**What would change it.** A controlled study showing that rankings stay stable across clean and noisy versions of the same benchmark.
input.new_string:
**Answer.** Yes, to a large extent. The main sources of variation are:
- **Wrong labels.** Only 39–65% of "vulnerable" labels in popular datasets are correct [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 48.8% in a PHP benchmark [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
- **Test data copied from training data.** Up to 18.9% exact copies [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Even when a PHP dataset was split by plugin, duplicate and contradictory-label groups still crossed the splits before cleaning [@tashenova2026real, p. 4].
- **Balanced vs realistic test sets.** The class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 8]. LLM F1 falls from about 49–65% to 5.41–12.21% when pairs are dropped [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- **Trivial baselines rarely reported.** Where they are reported, they are often competitive: a one-feature token-count rule matches learned models in PHP [@tashenova2026real, p. 8], and "flag everything" scores within reach of most LLMs [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @lu2025lab, p. 14].
- **Time and dataset shift.** Detectors trained on one dataset or period collapse on another [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13].
- **Prompt wording and decision threshold.** Either can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20].
- **Synthetic vs real code.** LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
- **Function-level vs line-level scoring.** Line-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
- **Custom datasets with inconsistent splits** [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Even a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11], so high scores on that dataset say little about real understanding. The same model on the same named dataset can differ by 28 F1 points between papers [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].

**Evidence strength: strong** for label noise and for the collapse of scores under realistic evaluation, which independent primary studies and two systematic reviews agree on [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. **Moderate** for prompt and threshold sensitivity and for trivial baselines, which rest on fewer studies.

**What would change it.** A controlled study showing that rankings stay stable across clean and noisy versions of the same benchmark, across prompts and across thresholds.

content.text: Now §3 (research questions).

input.old_string:
**Answer.** It depends on the setting:
- **Small, self-contained code.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on ten C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10], and a CASTLE score of 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- **Synthetic suites.** CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **Whole projects.** General coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST on C/C++ (59.55% vs 0–34.29%). Most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- **Against fine-tuned DL.** The ranking depends on the dataset and on the share of vulnerable samples [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. On PrimeVul pairs of vulnerable and fixed code, every family scores near or below chance [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].

**Evidence strength: weak to moderate.** The studies are mostly single runs, use five incompatible headline metrics, and cannot be pooled [I] (methodology comparison §3.5).

**What would change it.** A study that runs all three families on the same real, recent code with one shared metric (gap G2). Only khare2025understanding runs all three, and its SAST arm is on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7].
input.new_string:
**Answer.** It depends on the setting and on which score you use:
- **Small, self-contained code.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on ten C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10], and a CASTLE score of 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- **Synthetic suites.** CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **Whole projects.** General coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST on C/C++ (59.55% vs 0–34.29%). Most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- **All three families on the same real functions (new in pass 2).** deininger2026open tests 8 LLMs, 3 lightweight SAST tools and fine-tuned CodeBERT detectors on the same 1549 C/C++ functions from the PrimeVul dataset.
  - Seven of the eight LLMs, asked without examples (*zero-shot*), beat the SAST tools on *balanced accuracy*, a score that averages how well a tool handles vulnerable and safe code [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10].
  - A fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all eight LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
  - When the functions are re-scored at the dataset's natural mix (about 1 vulnerable function for every 44 safe ones, "1:44"), Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM. LLM precision is 2.3–4.6%, barely above the 2.21% of a rule that flags everything [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **Against fine-tuned DL elsewhere.** The ranking depends on the dataset, the share of vulnerable samples and the *decision threshold* (the score above which a model says "vulnerable") [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. On PrimeVul pairs of vulnerable and fixed code, every family scores near or below chance [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].
- **Recent code (new in pass 2).** On Linux and Chromium vulnerabilities disclosed from May 2025, where 1.97% of functions are vulnerable, trained DL detectors reach F1 3.47–8.65 and four open LLMs of up to 32B parameters reach 0.79–5.36 [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. By our calculation, a rule that flags everything would score about 3.87, so both families sit close to it [I].
- **PHP (new in pass 2).** No LLM has been tested on PHP in our corpus. The authors' own in-house analyser detects only 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins [@tashenova2026real, p. 9], which says nothing about established PHP SAST tools [I].

**Evidence strength: weak to moderate.** The studies are mostly single runs, use incompatible headline metrics, and cannot be pooled [I] (methodology comparison §3.5). Only one study compares all three families on identical real functions, and its SAST arm is lightweight: CodeQL could not be run on isolated functions [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. The most robust pattern [I] is that LLMs have higher recall and lower precision, and that at realistic prevalence their margin over trivial baselines is small.

**What would change it.** A study that runs all three families, including a *semantic* SAST tool such as CodeQL, on the same real code released after the models' training cutoff, with file or repository context and one shared metric (gap G2). khare2025understanding runs all three, but its SAST arm is on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]; deininger2026open uses pre-2023 CVEs and single functions [@deininger2026open, p. 24]. A preprint comparing LLMs, fine-tuned small models and SAST in Python, Java and JavaScript (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv 2503.01449; abstract only, not analysed) could extend the answer beyond C/C++ if added (§8).

**Answer.** Yes, to a large extent. The main sources of variation are:
- **Wrong labels.** Only 39–65% of "vulnerable" labels in popular datasets are correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- **Test data copied from training data.** Up to 18.9% exact copies [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4].
- **Balanced vs realistic test sets.** The class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. LLM F1 falls from about 49–65% to 5.41–12.21% when pairs are dropped [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- **Synthetic vs real code.** LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
- **Function-level vs line-level scoring.** Line-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
- **Custom datasets with inconsistent splits** [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Even a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11], so high scores on that dataset say little about real understanding.

**Evidence strength: moderate to strong.** Independent primary studies agree, and two systematic reviews concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].

**What would change it.** A controlled study showing that rankings stay stable across clean and noisy versions of the same benchmark.

**Answer.** Yes, to a large extent. The main sources of variation are:
- **Wrong labels.** Only 39–65% of "vulnerable" labels in popular datasets are correct [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 48.8% in a PHP benchmark [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
- **Test data copied from training data.** Up to 18.9% exact copies [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Even when a PHP dataset was split by plugin, duplicate and contradictory-label groups still crossed the splits before cleaning [@tashenova2026real, p. 4].
- **Balanced vs realistic test sets.** The class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 8]. LLM F1 falls from about 49–65% to 5.41–12.21% when pairs are dropped [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- **Trivial baselines rarely reported.** Where they are reported, they are often competitive: a one-feature token-count rule matches learned models in PHP [@tashenova2026real, p. 8], and "flag everything" scores within reach of most LLMs [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @lu2025lab, p. 14].
- **Time and dataset shift.** Detectors trained on one dataset or period collapse on another [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13].
- **Prompt wording and decision threshold.** Either can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20].
- **Synthetic vs real code.** LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
- **Function-level vs line-level scoring.** Line-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
- **Custom datasets with inconsistent splits** [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Even a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11], so high scores on that dataset say little about real understanding. The same model on the same named dataset can differ by 28 F1 points between papers [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].

**Evidence strength: strong** for label noise and for the collapse of scores under realistic evaluation, which independent primary studies and two systematic reviews agree on [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. **Moderate** for prompt and threshold sensitivity and for trivial baselines, which rest on fewer studies.

**What would change it.** A controlled study showing that rankings stay stable across clean and noisy versions of the same benchmark, across prompts and across thresholds.

- **Cost.** LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 for one project, while SAST takes minutes with no token cost [@li2026llm, p. 16].
  - The only *cost per true positive* (the cost of each real bug found) comes from a non-hybrid study: USD 0.003–0.212 and 3.7–119.6 kJ of energy per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8].
  - These are compute costs only. The analyst time needed to check the 25.6–41.9 false alarms that come with each real bug is not included [@deininger2026open, p. 8], and part of the energy values are estimates from operation counts (FLOP estimates), not measurements [@deininger2026open, p. 14].
  - Small open models can match a frontier model at 1/66 of the cost [@deininger2026open, p. 17]. **Strength: moderate, single study.**
- **Explainability.**

input.old_string:
1. **li2026llm** (TSE 2026) is the only independent, project-scale comparison of LLM detectors, agents and SAST tools that also reports cost. Read it to understand C2, C3 and C6 [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]. Be aware that it labels warnings partly with an LLM that it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11].
2. **risse2025top** (FSE 2025) shows that common benchmark labels are often wrong and that trivial classifiers score highly. It is the backbone of the "setup explains results" argument [@risse2025top, p. 8; @risse2025top, p. 11].
3. **ding2025vulnerability** (ICSE 2025, PrimeVul) audits label noise and duplication and introduces the vulnerable/patched pair test that defeats every model [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
4. **khare2025understanding** (ICST 2025) is the only study that runs LLMs, SAST and DL together, so it is the nearest thing to a three-way comparison [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @khare2025understanding, p. 9].
5. **kaniewski2026systematic** (TOSEM 2026) is the most current systematic review (263 studies). You must position your review against it [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].

1. **deininger2026open** (*Computers* 2026) is the only study that runs LLMs, SAST tools and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same real functions with the same metrics, and the only one that reports cost and energy per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. It also uses proper significance tests [@deininger2026open, p. 6] and shows how a reworded prompt or a default threshold can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. Be aware of its limits: lightweight SAST without CodeQL, CVEs from 2008–2022 that the LLMs may have seen in training, and single functions without context [@deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 24].

3. **lu2025lab** (JSS 2026) builds a test set of Linux and Chromium vulnerabilities disclosed from May 2025, after the evaluated models were released [@lu2025lab, p. 4]. On it, a DL detector that scores F1 91.00 on its own benchmark drops to 6.87 [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13], and open LLMs do no better. It is the clearest picture of what happens on genuinely new code. It has no SAST arm and runs each LLM once [@lu2025lab, p. 8].
4. **risse2025top** (FSE 2025) shows that common benchmark labels are often wrong and that trivial classifiers score highly. It is the backbone of the "setup explains results" argument [@risse2025top, p. 8; @risse2025top, p. 11].
5. **kaniewski2026systematic** (TOSEM 2026) is the most current systematic review (263 studies). You must position your review against it [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].

If you have time for two more: **ding2025vulnerability** (ICSE 2025, PrimeVul) audits label noise and duplication and introduces the vulnerable/patched pair test that defeats every model [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; **khare2025understanding** (ICST 2025) was the first study in our corpus to run LLMs, SAST and DL together, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @khare2025understanding, p. 9].

We found six contradictions (evidence matrix C1–C6). Each can be traced to a difference in setup. The explanations are our interpretation [I].

- **C1. Fine-tuned models vs GPT-4.**
  - What disagrees: on Big-Vul, fine-tuned models far exceed prompted GPT-4 (F1 94% and 87% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. On PrimeVul pairs, GPT-4 beats every fine-tuned model (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
  - Likely reason: the metric, the data split and the dataset cleaning differ. On pairs, every model is below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family.

We found eight contradictions (evidence matrix C1–C8; C7 and C8 are new in pass 2). Each can be traced, at least in part, to a difference in setup. The explanations are our interpretation [I].

- **C1. Fine-tuned models vs GPT-4.**
  - What disagrees: on Big-Vul, fine-tuned models far exceed prompted GPT-4 (F1 94% and 87% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. On PrimeVul pairs, GPT-4 beats every fine-tuned model (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Pass 2: on single, unpaired PrimeVul functions, a fine-tuned CodeBERT again beats all eight LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
  - Likely reason: the metric, the data split and the dataset cleaning differ. On pairs, every model is below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. The threshold matters too: with the default rule, deininger's fine-tuned detector looks like an "always safe" classifier although it ranks functions well (ROC-AUC 0.845) [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. Unpaired and pair results must not be pooled.

content.text: Now §4 and §5.

input.old_string:
1. **li2026llm** (TSE 2026) is the only independent, project-scale comparison of LLM detectors, agents and SAST tools that also reports cost. Read it to understand C2, C3 and C6 [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]. Be aware that it labels warnings partly with an LLM that it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11].
2. **risse2025top** (FSE 2025) shows that common benchmark labels are often wrong and that trivial classifiers score highly. It is the backbone of the "setup explains results" argument [@risse2025top, p. 8; @risse2025top, p. 11].
3. **ding2025vulnerability** (ICSE 2025, PrimeVul) audits label noise and duplication and introduces the vulnerable/patched pair test that defeats every model [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
4. **khare2025understanding** (ICST 2025) is the only study that runs LLMs, SAST and DL together, so it is the nearest thing to a three-way comparison [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @khare2025understanding, p. 9].
5. **kaniewski2026systematic** (TOSEM 2026) is the most current systematic review (263 studies). You must position your review against it [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].
input.new_string:
1. **deininger2026open** (*Computers* 2026) is the only study that runs LLMs, SAST tools and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same real functions with the same metrics, and the only one that reports cost and energy per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. It also uses proper significance tests [@deininger2026open, p. 6] and shows how a reworded prompt or a default threshold can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. Be aware of its limits: lightweight SAST without CodeQL, CVEs from 2008–2022 that the LLMs may have seen in training, and single functions without context [@deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 24].
2. **li2026llm** (TSE 2026) is the only independent, project-scale comparison of LLM detectors, agents and SAST tools that also reports cost. Read it to understand C2, C3 and C6 [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]. Be aware that it labels warnings partly with an LLM that it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11].
3. **lu2025lab** (JSS 2026) builds a test set of Linux and Chromium vulnerabilities disclosed from May 2025, after the evaluated models were released [@lu2025lab, p. 4]. On it, a DL detector that scores F1 91.00 on its own benchmark drops to 6.87 [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13], and open LLMs do no better. It is the clearest picture of what happens on genuinely new code. It has no SAST arm and runs each LLM once [@lu2025lab, p. 8].
4. **risse2025top** (FSE 2025) shows that common benchmark labels are often wrong and that trivial classifiers score highly. It is the backbone of the "setup explains results" argument [@risse2025top, p. 8; @risse2025top, p. 11].
5. **kaniewski2026systematic** (TOSEM 2026) is the most current systematic review (263 studies). You must position your review against it [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].

If you have time for two more: **ding2025vulnerability** (ICSE 2025, PrimeVul) audits label noise and duplication and introduces the vulnerable/patched pair test that defeats every model [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; **khare2025understanding** (ICST 2025) was the first study in our corpus to run LLMs, SAST and DL together, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @khare2025understanding, p. 9].

We found eight contradictions (evidence matrix C1–C8; C7 and C8 are new in pass 2). Each can be traced, at least in part, to a difference in setup. The explanations are our interpretation [I].

Unpaired and pair results must not be pooled.

content.text: Now §6 (gaps and positioning).

input.old_string:
All gaps passed a recorded novelty check on 2026-11-12. "No study found" means we found none in those searches, not that none exists.

| Gap | Confidence | Suggested study | Beginner feasibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G1.** Published results are never re-scored against trivial baselines ("flag everything") or realistic prevalence | medium–high | Re-compute MCC, ΔF1 vs flag-all, and precision at 1–17% prevalence from the published tables of the 16 primary studies | **easy** (spreadsheet, 2–4 weeks, no compute) |
| **G2.** No same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison on real code released after the models' training cutoff (*post-cutoff* code) | medium | ~100 post-cutoff + ~100 pre-cutoff Python or Java CVEs; Semgrep/CodeQL, a fine-tuned UniXcoder, 2–3 open LLMs | moderate (6–10 weeks) |
| **G3.** Loss of real bugs in LLM alarm filtering is not controlled per vulnerability type on real alerts | low–medium | Filter only the CWE types with low miss rates; tune on half of OWASP, test on the other half and on ~100 real alerts | easy–moderate (4–6 weeks) |
| **G4.** No independent, blinded replication of IRIS / RepoAudit | medium | 2 × 2 design: original vs new targets × original vs false-discovery metric, labelled by humans blinded to the tool | moderate–hard |
| **G5.** No repository-level, real-CVE LLM vs SAST evidence for PHP and Go | low–medium | ~60 real PHP or Go CVEs; Semgrep + 2 open LLMs | moderate |
| **G6.** No cost per confirmed vulnerability (compute + analyst triage time) across all three families | low–medium | Add to G2 as a secondary outcome | moderate |

Why G1 matters: on a 50/50 test set, flagging everything already gives F1 0.667. Several published best results sit at or just above that line. One example is a dummy classifier at 0.6693 vs a best model at 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]. Others are best F1 values of 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7] and GPT F1 values of 48–66 [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6]. Only one primary study applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count].

**Positioning of the review** (medium confidence). We found no review that combines (a) a synthesis across LLM, SAST and DL plus both hybrid types with (b) a setup-based explanation of specific contradictions. Reviews in the corpus are either LLM-only [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], predate most hybrid and project-scale work [@zhou2025large, p. 18], or are narrative [@sheng2025llms, p. 25]. The closest competitor outside the corpus is a 2026 review in *Computers and Artificial Intelligence* (doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137). We read only its abstract, which already raises the duplicates, label noise and leakage point, so the novelty claim must stay narrow.
input.new_string:
All gaps passed a recorded novelty check on 2026-11-12 and were re-checked in pass 2. "No study found" means we found none in those searches, not that none exists. Gaps are ranked by evidence strength and by how feasible they are for a beginner; **the top three for you are G1, G2 and G3**.

| Gap | After pass 2 | Confidence | Suggested study | Beginner feasibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **G1.** Published LLM, SAST and DL results are not re-scored *across studies* against trivial baselines ("flag everything") or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists | unchanged (premise strengthened) | medium–high | Re-compute MCC, ΔF1 vs flag-all, and precision at 1%, 5% and 17% prevalence from the published tables of the 20 primary studies; check the formulas against the studies that report their own baselines | **easy** (spreadsheet or ~50 lines of Python, 2–4 weeks, no compute) |
| **G2.** No same-benchmark LLM vs *semantic* SAST vs fine-tuned DL comparison on real code released after the models' training cutoff (*post-cutoff* code), with file or repository context | narrowed: a function-level, pre-cutoff C/C++ three-family study now exists (deininger2026open) | medium | ~100 post-cutoff + ~100 pre-cutoff Python or Java CVEs; Semgrep and CodeQL, a fine-tuned UniXcoder or CodeBERT, 2–3 open LLMs, plus flag-all. Cheaper variant: reuse the public 2025-CVE set from lu2025lab [@lu2025lab, p. 2] and add a SAST arm, an LLM arm with file context and a flag-all baseline | moderate (6–10 weeks) |
| **G3.** Loss of real bugs in LLM alarm filtering is not controlled per vulnerability type on real security alerts | unchanged | low–medium | Filter only the CWE types with low miss rates; tune on half of OWASP, test on the other half and on ~100 real alerts | easy–moderate (4–6 weeks) |
| **G4.** No independent, blinded replication of IRIS / RepoAudit that separates target, metric and labeller effects | unchanged | medium | 2 × 2 design: original vs new targets × original vs false-discovery metric, labelled by humans blinded to the tool | moderate–hard (an IRIS-only version on 20–30 CVEs: about 8 weeks) |
| **G5.** No real-CVE comparison of LLMs with *established* SAST tools for PHP and Go | narrowed: LLM-only WordPress evidence (Neef et al. 2026) and function-level Python/Java/JavaScript three-family evidence (Zhang et al. 2025) exist, both abstract only | low–medium | Reuse tashenova2026real's expert-verified PHP subset (125 vulnerable, 247 safe functions) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11] or ~60 Go CVEs; Semgrep plus a PHP or Go taint tool, 2 open LLMs, token-count and flag-all baselines | moderate |
| **G6.** No cost per *confirmed* vulnerability that includes analyst triage time and a costed SAST and DL arm on the same targets | narrowed: compute cost per true positive for 8 LLMs now exists (deininger2026open) | low–medium | Add to G2 as a secondary outcome: time two raters triaging 50 warnings per tool | moderate (piggybacks on G2) |

**Why G1 matters and why it is the easiest contribution.** On a 50/50 test set, flagging everything already gives F1 0.667. Several published best results sit at or just above that line: a dummy classifier at 0.6693 vs a best model at 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17], best F1 values of 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7] and GPT F1 values of 48–66 [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6]. Pass 2 shows the same at other prevalences:
- LLM F1 0.405–0.615 against 0.523 for "always vulnerable", and at 1:44 LLM precision only just above flag-all [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8];
- a one-feature token-count rule matching learned PHP detectors [@tashenova2026real, p. 8];
- 7 of 12 LLM F1 values on 2025 CVEs below the flag-all level, by our calculation [I] [@lu2025lab, p. 14].

These studies apply baselines only to their own results; none re-scores other studies' published numbers on a common scale [I]. Statistics are also rare: among the first 16 primary studies only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count]; of the four pass-2 papers, deininger2026open does [@deininger2026open, p. 6]. G1 needs only published tables and a spreadsheet, and the studies that report their own baselines give you a built-in check that your formulas are right. Credit those within-study baselines; the contribution is the *systematic cross-study* re-scoring.

**Positioning of the review** (medium confidence). We found no review that combines (a) a synthesis across LLM, SAST and DL plus both hybrid types with (b) a setup-based explanation of specific contradictions. Reviews in the corpus are either LLM-only [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], predate most hybrid and project-scale work [@zhou2025large, p. 18], or are narrative [@sheng2025llms, p. 25]. The closest competitor, qin2026review, has now been read in full. It shares our "evaluation reliability" framing [@qin2026review, p. 10] [A], but it reports no search protocol, puts SAST explicitly out of scope [@qin2026review, p. 4], and its numbers re-report papers already in our corpus [@qin2026review, p. 12; @qin2026review, p. 15], so it is not independent evidence [I]. content.text: Now §7 (limitations).

input.old_string:
- **Size.** 20 papers, chosen to keep the first pass manageable. This is a focused critical review, not a complete systematic review. Several relevant 2026 papers were found during gap checks but not analysed (§8).
- **Speed of the field.** Searches ran on 2026-11-12. Many near-miss studies appeared in 2026, so gaps G2, G3 and G5 could close soon.
- **Preprints and versions.**
  - zhou2024comparison is not peer-reviewed. Its per-language results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
  - Fifteen published papers were read from arXiv copies. du2026reducing came from an early version with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2], so it carries the highest risk that its numbers changed.
  - One paper's identity (ahmed2026secvuleval) is marked "unverified" by `rlab` because its title differs from the arXiv version. A reviewer confirmed it manually by its authors.
- **Independence.**
  - Three studies share the PrimeVul dataset family [I].
  - zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is its own authors' preprint [@zhou2025large, p. 22].
  - The independent project-scale study uses an LLM as labeller [@li2026llm, p. 11].
- **No pooling.** Metrics are too varied for a meta-analysis (a statistical combination of results), so our answers are narrative.
- **Language bias.** The evidence comes mostly from C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28].
- **Abstract-only material.** Statements about papers outside the corpus (§6, §8) are based on abstracts only.
input.new_string:
- **Size.** 24 papers (20 primary studies, 4 reviews). This is a focused critical review, not a complete systematic review. Several relevant papers were found during gap checks but not analysed, including a second three-family comparison (Zhang et al. 2025) that the pass-1 searches returned but we missed (§8).
- **Speed of the field.** Searches ran on 2026-11-12. Many near-miss studies appeared in 2026; pass 2 already narrowed G2, G5 and G6, and G3 could close soon too.
- **Search coverage.** The arXiv service timed out on 6 of the 9 pass-2 novelty searches (Q27–Q29 and Q31–Q33). We covered arXiv instead with one further arXiv search (Q34) and by reading the abstract pages of the two papers flagged for checking. Some recent arXiv preprints may still have been missed.
- **Corrections made in pass 2.** Some pass-1 gap notes were based on abstracts and turned out wrong once the full texts were read: deininger2026open *does* run SAST tools (the pass-1 notes said it did not), tashenova2026real is now read in full rather than known from its abstract, and lu2025lab turned out to be published in a journal. The gap report and this report now follow the full texts. [I] Abstract-based judgements about the papers still outside the corpus (§8) could be wrong in the same way.
- **Energy and cost figures.** Part of deininger2026open's energy per true positive comes from estimates based on counted operations (FLOP estimates), not from measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14], and that estimator overstates measured energy by 5.4–16.9× [@deininger2026open, p. 14]. Its cost figures also leave out human triage [@deininger2026open, p. 8]. Treat these numbers as rough orders of magnitude.
- **Preprints and versions.**
  - zhou2024comparison is not peer-reviewed. Its per-language results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
  - Fifteen published papers, plus lu2025lab (arXiv v4 accepted manuscript), were read from arXiv copies. du2026reducing came from an early version with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2], so it carries the highest risk that its numbers changed.
  - qin2026review's venue does not document peer review [@qin2026review, p. 1]; we use it for positioning only.
  - One paper's identity (ahmed2026secvuleval) is marked "unverified" by `rlab` because its title differs from the arXiv version. A reviewer confirmed it manually by its authors.
- **Independence.**
  - Four studies share the PrimeVul dataset family (ding, yildiz, tan, deininger) [I].
  - One of lu2025lab's four training datasets (ICVul) is the authors' own [@lu2025lab, p. 3].
  - qin2026review re-reports papers already in our corpus, so it adds no independent support [@qin2026review, p. 12].
  - zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is its own authors' preprint [@zhou2025large, p. 22].
  - The independent project-scale study uses an LLM as labeller [@li2026llm, p. 11].
- **Single runs and prompts.** Most primary studies run each model once. deininger2026open shows that rewording the prompt can move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 19; @deininger2026open, p. 20], so small differences elsewhere should not be over-read [I].
- **No pooling.** Metrics are too varied for a meta-analysis (a statistical combination of results), so our answers are narrative.
- **Language bias.** The evidence comes mostly from C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]; PHP rests on one study with no LLM arm [@tashenova2026real, p. 13].
- **Abstract-only material.** Statements about papers outside the corpus (§6, §8) are based on abstracts only.
- **Record keeping.** The `metadata.json` files of three pass-2 papers carry a wrong, shared reason for inclusion; the correct reasons are in `search/screening.md`. This does not affect any finding.

input.old_string: - **SAST (static application security testing):** tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep that scan code with hand-written rules without running it.
input.new_string:
- **XSS (cross-site scripting):** a web vulnerability where an attacker gets their script to run in other users' browsers.
- **SAST (static application security testing):** tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep that scan code with hand-written rules without running it.
- **Lightweight vs semantic SAST:** lightweight tools (e.g. Flawfinder, Cppcheck) match patterns in the text of the code; semantic tools (e.g. CodeQL) build a model of the whole program and track how data flows through it, which usually requires building the project.
- **Taint analysis:** a SAST technique that follows untrusted input ("tainted" data) to see whether it reaches a dangerous operation.

- **Taint analysis:** a SAST technique that follows untrusted input ("tainted" data) to see whether it reaches a dangerous operation.

input.old_string:
- **F1:** a single score that balances precision and recall.
- **False-positive rate (FPR):** the share of safe code wrongly flagged as vulnerable.
input.new_string:
- **F1:** a single score that balances precision and recall. *Macro F1* averages the F1 of the "vulnerable" and "safe" classes.
- **False-positive rate (FPR):** the share of safe code wrongly flagged as vulnerable.
- **Specificity:** the share of safe code that the tool correctly leaves alone (1 − FPR).
- **Balanced accuracy:** the average of recall and specificity, so a tool cannot score well just by always giving the majority answer.
- **ROC-AUC:** how well a model ranks vulnerable code above safe code across all possible thresholds; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
- **Decision threshold:** the score above which a model's output is counted as "vulnerable"; changing it trades recall against precision.
- **Cost per true positive:** the money or energy spent for each real vulnerability a tool finds.
- **FLOP estimate:** an energy figure calculated from the number of computing operations a model needs, rather than measured on the hardware.

## 1. Summary in plain language

We asked whether large language models (LLMs, such as GPT-4 or Claude) find security bugs in source code better than two older approaches: rule-based scanners (SAST tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep) and neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code (deep-learning or "DL" detectors). After reading 24 papers in full, the short answer is still that **no approach wins everywhere**: LLMs come out ahead on small, self-contained programs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], CodeQL on synthetic test suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9], and on large real projects both miss many bugs and raise many false alarms [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. The only study that tests all three families on the same real functions finds that the winner depends on the score you choose: a fine-tuned DL model has the best overall score, two of the scanners are the most precise (their warnings are least often false alarms), and the LLMs sit in between [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. The most consistent pattern [I] is that LLMs find more of the real bugs (higher recall) but also flag much more harmless code (lower precision); when vulnerable code is as rare as in real software (about 2% of functions), their precision is barely better than a rule that flags everything, and on vulnerabilities from 2025 trained DL detectors do little better [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. A large part of the disagreement between papers comes from **how** they test, not from the tools themselves: label quality, overlap between training and test data, the share of vulnerable samples, and how lenient the scoring is [@risse2025top, p. 8; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. Letting an LLM filter a scanner's alarms removes most false alarms cheaply but also throws away 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. For your comparative review, this "setup explains the contradictions" angle, applied across all three families, is still the contribution we could not find in existing reviews (medium confidence). The easiest concrete addition is to re-score the published results against a "flag everything" baseline, which needs only a spreadsheet.
